newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedes turn to illegal booze as smuggling surges.
newsitem.headline: Swedes turn to illegal booze as smuggling surges.

text.p: Strict controls designed to curb alcohol consumption in Sweden are starting to wobble, adding weight to calls for the government to get off the wagon.

A government monopoly on the sale of alcohol in Sweden has come under fire this month, with a European court adviser saying it was an obstacle to EU law and a poll showing Swedes want the state to loosen its grip on the hard stuff.

The European Court of Justice's Advocate-General Michael Elmer said he would recommend that the court order Sweden to end its monopoly and a recent survey showed two out of three citizens want to end state alcohol control.
Swedes are tired of queueing at monopoly Systembolaget's stores during business hours and paying 204 crowns ($27) for the cheapest bottle of whisky in the store.
Bottom-of-the-range wine costs about 50 crowns in the government store and as much as three times that amount in a Stockholm restaurant. SWEDES TURN INTO MOONSHINERS AND SMUGGLERS
Heavy sales taxes on alcohol have pushed the prices of spirits, wine and even beer sky-high, but Swedes are finding their own ways to beat booze prices.
These include smuggling, home brewing, and even downing pure spirits -- occasionally with fatal consequences.

"It would clean the air if the government would admit it has lost control of the alcohol market," wrote Kjell-Olof Feldt, former finance minister and chairman of a wine and spirits association, in a recent newspaper column.
Although different monopolies have controlled Swedes' drinking habits for almost 200 years, the picture has changed since Sweden joined the European Union in January 1995.
However, the minority Social Democratic government is still fighting to protect people's health by keeping down alcohol consumption.

The government has ended wholesaler Vin & Sprit's monopoly on alcohol distribution since joining the EU but it has managed to extend until July 1, 2000, a Swedish exemption from liberalised European personal import allowances.

Other EU members can bring 110 litres of beer, 90 litres of wine and 10 litres of spirits home from their trips abroad, but Swedes are allowed only 15 litres of beer and the choice of five litres of table wine and one litre of spirits, or three litres of strong wine and no spirits.
Normally upright Swedes are ducking these restrictions.

Illegal alcohol is flooding into the country in trucks and railway carriages from other EU countries which do not require travellers to show documents at the border with Sweden. RELAXED EU BORDERS BRING FLOOD OF CONTRABAND
"It is a bit of a Klondike now with the free movement of goods," Egon Jacobsson, the head of state-owned alcohol wholesaler Vin & Sprit (Wine and Spirit), told Reuters.

Director General of Customs Ulf Larsson said his officers seized around seven times more illicit alcohol in 1996 than in previous years, confiscating 500,000 litres against around 60,000 litres in each of the previous three years.
However, authorities are well aware that most shipments still slip through the net. Jacobsson estimated that roughly half of all the alcohol sold in Sweden was illegal.
"Reports have shown that there are organised gangs, with a widespread, well-functioning network, that smuggle spirits into Sweden," Jacobsson said.
Gabriel Romanus, Systembolaget's head, said that legal consumption had decreased, possibly as a result of increased smuggling.
In 1996, sales at the 395 Systembolaget stores across Sweden fell by around one billion crowns ($130 million) to about 19 billion crowns.
To curb alcohol consumption, the stores keep limited hours and stay closed all weekend.
Furthermore, anyone buying alcohol from Systembolaget has to be over 20 years old -- even though Swedes have the right to vote and drive at 18 and have sex at 15.
CHEAP TIPPLES CAN BE FATAL
The government also levies taxes of between 80 and 90 percent of the total sales price on alcohol, making a 70 centilitre bottle of the cheapest hard liquor cost 157 crowns.
In comparison, a smuggled "brand name" one litre bottle costs around 100 crowns and the same amount of moonshine booze costs from 80 to 90 crowns, Jacobsson said.

Poisonous methanol, used in industry and which tastes, smells and looks just like vodka, is even cheaper at 30 crowns a litre. Casualties from drinks spiked with a little methanol, or even from pure methanol, are increasing.
During New Year celebrations this year, a 20-year-old man died and five of his friends needed hospital treatment after drinking a bottle of pure methanol stolen from a publishing house.
The rise in smuggled alcohol has put authorities in a spin, destroying the state's attempts to maintain a hangover-free society.
"My personal estimate is that total consumption increases when there is such easy access to alcohol on the illegal market, which is open 24 hours a day," Jacobsson said.
Although opposition to the alcohol rules is growing, many still support government controls which they see as well-intended.
"Many of those calling for tax cuts have commercial interests in the business," Romanus said. "They show propaganda figures to frighten the government into lowering taxes." ($ = 7.629 Swedish Crowns)
